title: Is It Up to You?
hook: Beside the rejection email, a designer draws one line between verdict and craft.
counterintuition: Control grows smaller when you chase verdicts. It grows sharper when you spend effort only on the part your conduct can touch.
tryThisNow: Draw two columns for one live problem: yours to choose and not yours to command. Move one task from the second column back to reality.
keyTakeaway: Ask what is up to you before you spend force, then place effort only where choice, preparation, conduct, and response remain available.

breakdown.fastRead:
Tracing paper rasps under Grace's hand as she rereads the client's rejection. The public result is simple: the proposal lost. Her private correction is harder: the typography was rushed, the case study was thin, and the client's taste was never hers to command.

Control begins at the boundary. Grace cannot make the client prefer her style, award the contract, or admire her portfolio. She can repair the portfolio page, log the weak pitch, and send a cleaner sample next time.

The question is not whether the outcome hurts. It is whether her next ounce of effort belongs on the verdict or on the craft.
breakdown.deepRead:
"We did everything," Andrew hears outside the ward room, and the sentence lands like a verdict. The family is waiting for an update, the printed rounding schedule is already late, and the consultant needs a decision before noon. Andrew wants the outcome to be proof that he did enough. He also wants it to be proof that no one could have done more. Both wishes pull him away from the boundary.

He writes two headings on the back of the schedule.

Under his choice, he lists the bedside explanation, the medication check, the handoff note, and whether he speaks plainly to the family. Under external, he lists disease course, timing, bed availability, and the family's reaction. The division does not absolve him. It assigns him. A control boundary is not an excuse to care less; it is a way to care where care can still become conduct.

Some facts do not take orders.

Andrew walks back to the family with the part that belongs to him: clear language, no hiding, no defensive performance. He cannot decide the response waiting on the other side of the conversation. He can decide whether his part of the room is truthful, prepared, and humane.
breakdown.fullRead:
The gym corridor smells faintly of floor wax after tryouts. Giulia's name is not on the posted roster, and the selection rule cannot be changed after the coaches sign the sheet. A line of players waits near the equipment cage, each pretending not to stare. Giulia has a marked-up training form folded in her pocket and a voice in her head that wants to argue with the door.

She opens the form instead. One column is selection. That belongs to the coaches. Another is attendance. That belongs to her. A third is repeatable skill: left-foot passing, defensive recovery, sprint starts. That also belongs to her. The boundary does not make the cut kinder. It stops the cut from consuming the next practice.

What part of this can be governed by your choice? Ask it with enough precision that the answer can be seen. Not "my attitude," which is too foggy. Try "the email I send," "the form I revise," "the apology I make," "the reps I complete," "the evidence I gather," or "the tone I use when the ruling goes against me."

Antoine faces that last version at a housing tribunal. You sit beside him in a row of empty chairs after the hearing, with the office door locked for lunch and a backup route to the clerk's desk closing in two minutes. He must decide whether to spend those minutes rehearsing the unfairness of the landlord's testimony or filing the missing repair photos. The ruling is not his to command. The tone of the follow-up and the completeness of the record are still his.

That is the useful cut between control and fantasy. Fantasy says that enough effort should force other people to approve, heal, buy, select, forgive, or agree. Control says effort deserves to be placed where it can become action. You can prepare the demo. You cannot make the buyer's quarter open. You can lower your voice. You cannot make the teenager answer. You can check the form. You cannot make the clerk like your case.

It took Chidi three lost deals to see the difference. A stack of procurement notices sat unopened on a shelf when he reviewed the sales file. One spreadsheet row showed strong demo attendance. A timestamped note showed the buyer's budget freeze two hours before procurement review. The disputed fact was whether the demo had failed or the buying window had closed. Chidi still found work that belonged to him: tighten the security slide, write a clearer technical handoff, and stop treating every delayed deal as proof of weak skill.

Control is not always comforting. Sometimes the controllable portion is small, tedious, and unglamorous. It may be one sentence, one call, one apology, one revised checklist. But small is not the same as powerless. A small controllable action is cleaner than a large fantasy of command.

Anke sees it at home with the old plan half erased from the whiteboard. A weather alert has canceled the school trip, the supply box for the project sits in the hall, and the call list of parents is still unfinished. Her teenager has shut down behind a closed bedroom door. What is actually up to her? Not the weather, not the canceled trip, not whether the teenager talks immediately. She can lower the temperature in her own voice, make the parent calls, and leave one specific invitation on the table: help sort the project supplies at five.

The boundary gives effort a place to land. Without it, you push on weather, verdicts, moods, and timing as if they were levers. With it, you stop bargaining with what will not move and begin working on what is still yours.

examples.title: Grace Separates Verdict From Craft

planSpec.domain: freelance designer separating client taste from portfolio effort
planSpec.audience: Readers facing freelance design rejection who need to sort choice from verdict
planSpec.stakes: A lost contract can become wasted force on taste or useful force on craft.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Grace sorts the page into controllable craft and uncontrollable client verdict.

examples.scenario: Tracing paper rasps under Grace's palm while the rejection email stays open beside three sample sleeves. The public result is a lost contract. Her practice log gives the private correction: two thin case studies, a rushed type scale, and no control over the client's taste. In the postmortem, she draws a hard line between improving the portfolio and trying to command approval.
examples.whatToDo: Revise the weak case study and type scale, then leave the client's preference outside the work column.
examples.whyItMatters: The boundary stops Grace from wasting effort on a verdict while still holding her responsible for the craft she can improve.

examples.title: Andrew Writes Two Headings

planSpec.domain: medical resident sorting patient outcome from bedside conduct
planSpec.audience: Readers facing medical uncertainty who need to act where conduct remains available
planSpec.stakes: Confusing outcome with conduct can create either false guilt or false relief.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Andrew sorts bedside conduct from external medical outcome.

examples.scenario: "The family is waiting," the nurse says while Andrew checks the printed rounding schedule. The noon update is fixed, and the consultant needs him to decide how to speak before entering the room. Before the sort, Andrew treats the outcome as a verdict on his worth. After the sort, he owns the medication check, handoff note, and plain explanation, while leaving disease course outside command.
examples.whatToDo: Prepare the explanation, verify the handoff, and speak clearly. Do not use the family's reaction as the measure of whether he did his part.
examples.whyItMatters: Patient outcomes matter deeply, but not every part of them is governed by one resident's choice.

examples.title: Giulia Opens the Training Form

planSpec.domain: student athlete splitting practice reps from selection decision
planSpec.audience: Readers facing selection decisions who need a clean effort boundary
planSpec.stakes: A roster decision can freeze practice or make the next reps specific.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Giulia separates the selection rule from the reps she can still complete.

examples.scenario: The equipment cage rattles as the roster sheet goes up, and a visible line of players waits for jerseys. Giulia's name is missing. The selection rule cannot be changed, but the marked-up training form in her pocket still names left-foot passing, recovery runs, and attendance. In reflection, she sees the difference: the coaches own the list; she owns the next block of reps.
examples.whatToDo: Put the roster in the external column and put repeatable skills in the choice column. Schedule the first practice block before arguing with the outcome.
examples.whyItMatters: The cut is painful, but practicing the controllable skill keeps effort attached to something real.

examples.title: Antoine Uses the Two Minutes

planSpec.domain: landlord dispute where tone is controllable and ruling is not
planSpec.audience: Readers facing official decisions who need to keep force on record and conduct
planSpec.stakes: Two minutes can go into anger about the ruling or into the missing evidence.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Antoine sorts tone and record from the uncontrollable ruling.

examples.scenario: You sit beside Antoine in a row of empty chairs after the housing hearing, with the office door locked and a backup route to the clerk's desk closing in two minutes. He must decide whether to replay the landlord's testimony or submit repair photos before the window closes. Thought experiment: which action belongs to his choice, and which part belongs to the ruling?
examples.whatToDo: Use the two minutes to file the photos and keep his follow-up tone exact. Leave the ruling outside his command.
examples.whyItMatters: Anger at the verdict may be understandable, but the record is the only lever still in his hand.

examples.title: Chidi Reads the Budget Note

planSpec.domain: sales engineer distinguishing demo quality from buyer timing
planSpec.audience: Readers facing buyer delays who need to separate work quality from external timing
planSpec.stakes: A lost deal can become false self-blame or a sharper demo repair.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Chidi sorts demo quality from buyer timing.

examples.scenario: It took Chidi three lost deals to stop reading every silence as a failed demo. In the review room, one spreadsheet row shows nine engineers attended, and a timestamped note says the buyer froze budget before procurement met. He must decide whether the disputed fact is skill failure or timing. The answer leaves him one owned task: revise the security handoff.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the buyer's budget window from the demo materials. Improve the security handoff without pretending he controls procurement timing.
examples.whyItMatters: The boundary protects him from both excuses and false blame; it points effort at the part he can actually repair.

examples.title: Anke Leaves One Invitation

planSpec.domain: parent resetting conduct after a teenager shuts down
planSpec.audience: Readers facing family shutdowns who need to sort response from another person's mood
planSpec.stakes: A parent's effort can become pressure for an immediate answer or steadier conduct.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Anke sorts her tone and next action from the teenager's immediate response.

examples.scenario: What belongs to Anke after the door closes? The hallway whiteboard has the old plan half erased, a weather alert has canceled the school trip, and the project supply box blocks the stairs. The parent call list is unfinished. She must decide whether to push for an answer now or lower her voice, make the calls, and leave one specific invitation to sort supplies at five.
examples.whatToDo: Own tone, calls, and the clear invitation. Do not treat the teenager's immediate silence as a lever she can pull.
examples.whyItMatters: The boundary keeps care active without turning another person's mood into something she tries to command.

questions.prompt: A freelance designer loses a contract after a client says the style is not a fit. Her notes show two weak case studies and one rushed typography choice. What belongs in her control column?
choices: Convincing the client to prefer her visual style after the decision.
Revising the case studies and type scale before the next pitch.
Deciding that the rejection proves she should stop pitching.
questions.explanation: The craft revisions belong to her choice. Client taste and a final verdict do not. Quitting treats the verdict as total instead of sorting it.

questions.prompt: A medical resident is devastated after a patient outcome worsens. Which response best respects the boundary between outcome and conduct?
choices: Use the family's reaction as the only measure of whether he did enough.
Tell himself nothing mattered because disease course is external.
Verify the handoff, prepare the explanation, and speak truthfully to the family.
questions.explanation: Handoff, preparation, and truthful speech remain in his control. The family's reaction and the full disease course matter, but they are not levers he commands.

questions.prompt: A student athlete misses the roster after tryouts. The selection rule is final, but her training form shows weak sprint starts and missed recovery reps. What should she do?
choices: Put selection outside command and schedule the first block of repeatable reps.
Argue until the coaches admit the selection rule is unfair.
Treat the roster as proof that further practice cannot matter.
questions.explanation: The roster decision is external once final, while repeatable reps still belong to her. Arguing and quitting both spend force away from the available lever.

questions.prompt: Tenant has two minutes before the clerk's desk closes after a tense hearing. He cannot change the ruling today, but he has missing repair photos. Which action fits the control boundary?
choices: Replay the landlord's testimony so he can sharpen his anger.
File the photos and keep the follow-up note exact.
Wait for the ruling before completing the record.
questions.explanation: The photos and tone of the note are still his to choose. Rehearsing anger and waiting both abandon the small lever still available before the desk closes.

questions.prompt: Sales engineer loses a deal after a strong technical demo. A timestamped note shows the buyer froze budget before procurement review. What is the strongest analysis?
choices: The demo must have failed because the deal was lost.
The buyer's timing proves the whole sales process is pointless.
Budget timing is external, while demo materials and handoff quality remain reviewable.
questions.explanation: The note separates external timing from owned materials. Calling the demo failed ignores evidence, and calling the process pointless treats one external as total.

questions.prompt: Parent faces a teenager's silence after a canceled school trip. The weather is fixed, the teen's mood is not commandable, and parent calls remain unfinished. What should the parent own?
choices: Tone, parent calls, and one clear invitation for later help.
The teenager's immediate willingness to talk.
The weather cancellation and at any pointy emotional reaction to it.
questions.explanation: Tone, calls, and a specific invitation are conduct. The teen's immediate response and the weather are not controlled by parental force.

questions.prompt: Project lead says, "If I work hard enough, I can make leadership approve the plan." Which correction best protects useful effort?
choices: Treat the slip as effort decay rather than skill gap, so the supervisor's instinct toward pressure looks partly justified.
Approval is irrelevant, so the plan should be abandoned.
Preparation, evidence, and delivery are controllable; leadership's verdict is not.
questions.explanation: The correction keeps effort on the parts the lead can govern. More pressure confuses effort with command, while abandonment throws away real controllable work.

questions.prompt: Commuter is stuck after a signal failure. She cannot move the train, but she has a deadline, a phone signal, and a colleague who can receive notes. What is the best control-boundary move?
choices: Keep refreshing the train app until the signal failure changes.
Send the key notes to the colleague and update the deadline owner.
Decide the whole day is ruined because the train is late.
questions.explanation: Sending notes and updating the deadline owner are available actions. Refreshing the app and declaring the day ruined spend attention on what she cannot move.

questions.prompt: Grant applicant receives no answer from a funder for six weeks. He can revise the next application, request confirmation of receipt, or keep guessing about the committee's motives. What should he choose?
choices: Request confirmation and revise the next application materials.
Spend the week interpreting the committee's silence.
Assume silence proves the project is unworthy.
questions.explanation: Confirmation and revision are concrete choices. Guessing at motives and treating silence as proof both move effort into territory he cannot verify or command.

reviewCards.front: A situation hurts, but the outcome is outside command. What question starts the sort?
reviewCards.back: Ask what is up to you: choice, conduct, preparation, effort, tone, evidence, or response.

reviewCards.front: A verdict goes against you. What should move into the external column?
reviewCards.back: Move the verdict, other people's taste, timing, and approval outside command. Keep your next preparation and conduct inside choice.

reviewCards.front: Why is the control boundary not an excuse?
reviewCards.back: It does not reduce responsibility. It assigns responsibility precisely, so effort lands where it can become action.

reviewCards.front: What is the danger of treating outcomes as controllable?
reviewCards.back: You waste force on verdicts, weather, timing, and other people's reactions while neglecting the smaller action still available.

reviewCards.front: A controllable action feels too small to matter. How does taking a small controllable action change the field of available next moves?
reviewCards.back: Small does not mean powerless. One call, note, apology, checklist, or rep is stronger than a fantasy of command.

implementationPlan.title: Drawing the Boundary Around What You Control
implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is sorting before effort. You divide the situation into what belongs to choice and what belongs to externals, then act on the first item in the choice column.

ifThenPlans.plan: If approval is uncertain, then separate evidence and delivery from the final verdict before sending the next version.
If a grade or selection goes against you, then list the next practice behavior before arguing with the result.
If an outcome scares you, then identify the appointment, question, medication check, or conversation you can actually complete.
If someone else's mood dominates the room, then choose your tone, timing, and next sentence without demanding their response.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Today, draw a boundary for one frustrating situation. Circle one item in the choice column and complete it before revisiting the external column.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review a frustration that drained you. Mark where you chased an external and what controllable action deserved that energy.

memorableLines.why: It names the chapter's core sort in one sentence.

memorableLines.text: Some facts do not take orders.
memorableLines.why: It gives the external column a memorable edge.

memorableLines.text: The boundary gives effort a place to land.
memorableLines.why: It explains why the control sort is practical rather than passive.
